book: 148 - Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections

chapters.file: ch32 - Two Philosophies, Two Compasses to Navigate Life.md
chapters.relation: Against 'Hang the DJ,' where Frank and Amy's coaching system assigns partners and expiration dates inside a simulated dating park, the chapter argues a Stoic would refuse to sign up: delegating judgments to the coach violates Epictetus's dichotomy of control, and the endless date-cycle fails all four virtues, treating dates (like Amy's bored lovemaking) as means rather than inherently worthy persons. An existentialist reading via Sartre says nearly every system-arranged relationship is bad faith - couples act as if compatible against the expiry they were given, as Frank and Nicola do - and only Frank and Amy's open-ended, freely chosen relationship escapes it, so their 'fuck off' to the system is a leap of faith that 998 of 1000 simulated couples make, which is how the app computes its 99.8% match. The authors close with Camus's absurd, doubting that the real Frank and Amy, who cannot rebel against an app that tells them they belong together, will fare as well as their simulations.

The chapter asks whether the technophobia of 'Metalhead' - robo-dogs hunting Bella and her friends across a wasteland - is justified, testing Daniel Dinello's list of fears (identity, values, emotion, freedom, life). Descartes's and Aquinas's human-uniqueness over the mechanical fails because the robo-dogs, like DeepMind, learn and problem-solve, while the episode's Rousseau-style romanticism (only the non-technological cliff, tree, sunlight and stream aid Bella) and the teddy-bear mission show technology amplifying compassion rather than threatening it. The real dangers are robots as Latourian 'black boxes': Asimov's Three Laws cannot be operationalized, and if we cannot know how robo-dogs decide, our frameworks for blame and punishment break down (who answers for a killing - robot, programmer, or, on Marx's analysis of capitalist technology as an instrument of oppression, the economic system behind it?). The chapter concludes that since we already share the world with robots, learning to live responsibly alongside them must replace simple fear.

The chapter asks whether Nish's revenge in 'Black Museum' - poisoning Rolo and downloading his digital self into her father Clayton's eternal-electrocution exhibit - is morally justified. Nussbaum's Anger and Forgiveness condemns payback as sadism plus 'magical thinking' and prescribes transition-anger, then unconditional forgiveness, then best of all unconditional love (the prodigal son); Christian agape commands loving enemies and leaving wrath to God; and the Buddhist analysis of dukkha, karma and non-self shows Nish's hateful revenge generates worse karma than Rolo's greed and deepens the very suffering it means to end. The verdict: revenge, however emotionally satisfying, is never justified - even the tourists zapping Clayton and Nish zapping Rolo fall into the same trap.

Written as a choose-your-own-adventure whose branches mirror Bandersnatch's, the chapter treats you, the Netflix viewer, as the external force Stefan suspects: Libet-style readiness-potential neuroscience suggests conscious choice is an after-the-fact story, and compatibilist rescues (Frankfurt's second-order desires, Fischer's guidance control) founder on the 'BundyBot' argument that programmed desires are not freedom. Everett's many-worlds interpretation supplies the multiverse of 'one reality for each possible course of action,' and David Lewis's fixed-past block universe answers the grandfather paradox raised by Stefan's mirror-trip to die on the 8:45 train with his mother. Aristotle does double duty: the Poetics explains why Bandersnatch rightly limits your options (Sartrean absolute freedom would make a crappy story), and the Nicomachean Ethics on voluntary action pins moral responsibility for Stefan's murders on the viewer rather than the coerced Stefan. Adorno's culture industry asks whether Tuckersoft's 'hit factory' - and Black Mirror itself - can produce genuine art, while Kierkegaard's dread of irreversible choice is overturned by an episode that always lets you go back and try again.

Reading 'Striking Vipers' through its closed- and open-door imagery, the chapter asks whether Danny and Karl's virtual sex as Lance and Roxette is adultery, testing the question with Plato's Ring of Gyges (what people do when no one can see them), Locke's memory theory (if Danny remembers Roxette's sex acts, is Roxette Danny?), and behaviorist replies that only physical penetration counts. Nietzsche supplies the chapter's frame: his master/slave morality and his view of life as self-created representational art explain how the characters' hidden, mind-only moral inversion creates real existential meaning in virtual sex. The episode's fusion of bodily and mental pleasure is said to break down Mill's higher/lower pleasures distinction - 'lower' physical virtual pleasures yield a 'higher' sense of wholeness - and Schopenhauer's insatiable striving plus Husserl's meaning-conferring perception underwrite the conclusion that virtual love can be real, with Danny and Theo's once-a-year open marriage endorsed as an act-consequentialist balance between monotonous fidelity and escapist fantasy.

chapters.file: ch39 - “He’s done tech detox weekends here and there, but ten days ”.md
chapters.relation: Reading Smithereens as today's reality rather than a dystopia, the chapter explains the crash that killed Chris's fiancée through Herbert Simon's attention economy: platforms like Smithereen are free because they harvest and sell attention, and Billy Bauer admits the app was deliberately tuned 'like a crack pipe' with dopamine targets. Using Marx's analysis of capitalist surplus, the chapter argues (with Zuboff's 'behavioral surplus' and Crary's 24/7 capitalism) that users are wageless laborers generating value for free, and that compulsive checking is Gerald Moore's 'dopamining' - brain plasticity exploited by a hostile attention environment - rather than free choice. It rejects individual tech-detox consumerism as a false solution and closes with Simondon: knowing our machines is the beginning of the political reflection needed to dissolve the alienating 'fetishism of the tool.'

chapters.file: ch40 - “Oh, honey, I’ll do anything for you”.md
chapters.relation: Using Rachel's Ashley Too doll, the chapter distinguishes robots as instruments (Kevin's MAUZR mouse) from social robots designed to be perceived 'as being present in the way a person is,' and invokes Heidegger's 'Question Concerning Technology' to argue that social robots break the instrumentalist picture: it is our empathy - triggered even by the insubstantial hologram Ashley Eternal - that they exploit. The Aristotelian test of friendship (we emulate those we admire, and friendship forms virtuous character) shows Ashley Too fails: her flattery installs false confidence, and because she never requires Rachel to attend to another's needs, she models no real friendship. Girard's mimetic desire explains Rachel's borrowed aspiration to become Ashley O and Jack's emulation of their dead mother, so the chapter concludes robot 'friends' are poor friends - not because they are machines, but because a real friendship is 'an education in the social virtues.'

Focusing on White Christmas's cookies and Ashley Too's synaptic snapshot, the chapter argues behavior can never settle whether an artificial system is conscious: the Turing test fails against Geminoid-robot-style cases where recorded signals produce human-like behavior, and philosophical-zombie possibilities plus the point that computations and information patterns are subjective interpretations (not objective physical properties) mean only discovering the physical neural correlates of consciousness could tell us whether a cookie feels pain. It then separates copying from transferring: with souls and substance dualism rejected, Black Museum's 'transfers' are really copies, and San Junipero's upload would house a copy whose future experiences are as alien to Yorkie as a plaster cast of her feet. Ethically, if cookies are conscious, then Matt's breaking of Cookie-Greta, Daly's captives, and Clayton's keychain are torture of persons, and it is the very uncertainty about cookie consciousness that lets characters rationalize the abuse - which is why the in-world legislation granting cookies human rights matters.

The chapter asks 'Is your cookie you?', running theories of personal identity through Black Mirror's copies: the soul theory surfaces when Clayton signs away his 'digital self'; Locke's memory theory implies Cookie-Greta is Greta - a reductio, since one person cannot be wholly in two places at once (the same problem for Ashley Too and the thousand Hang the DJ simulations) - and the perdurantist patch recasts Greta and her cookie as time-slices of one four-dimensional person. Physical theories (Olson's animalism, Unger's brain-essentialism) rule out survival by upload, so Yorkie dies when her body dies even though digital Yorkie continues in San Junipero; Parfit's no-self bundle view and the teletransporter case then dissolve the fear, since there is no ego to lose and ordinary survival is 'about as bad' as being destroyed and replaced by a replica. The upshot: the punishment and immortality plots (Joe's million-year Christmas loop, San Junipero) require cookies to be both conscious and psychologically connected in the right way, and the episodes' horror depends on leaving that genuinely uncertain.

Reading Black Mirror's deaths through Bandersnatch's train ending, Be Right Back's AshBot, and San Junipero, the chapter uses Heidegger's presence-at-hand (Stefan's absent mother and rabbit remain present as possibilities he can act on) and Derrida's différance (the meaning of life and death is endlessly deferred as technology scrambles the presence/absence binary - Martha's simulated Ash, Liam's Grain deletions, Chris's guilt-haunted fiancée). A central section frames the whole debate as transhumanism - Kurzweil's three bridges to the posthuman against Fukuyama's warning that self-directed evolution replaces God - before Camus resolves the question of meaning: Kelly and Yorkie, like Sisyphus, create meaning by choosing their fate in a VR heaven that objectively matters nothing. Freud's Eros/Thanatos drives and Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' close the chapter's question of whether to extend, hasten, or simply accept mortality.

chapters.file: ch45 - Anti‐love Shows What Love Is.md
chapters.relation: The chapter takes Irma Thomas's 'Anyone Who Knows What Love Is (Will Understand)?' - the song Brooker plants across five episodes - as the key to the series, defining love with Aquinas (to love is to wish the good by which the beloved flourishes, rooted in proper self-love, on an Aristotelian base) and evil as the void left where that good is withheld. Each episode that plays the song features characters who mishear it: Hot Shot's judges take Abi's sacrificial love song as an audition for submission to WraithBabes, Joe misreads Beth's song as meant for him and kills Beth's father in the resulting void, and Mia in Crocodile refuses the self-sacrificing loving act of confessing, murdering to fill the gap. Callow's pig-for-a-princess self-sacrifice, Theo's speech about commitment, and digital Walton dying to protect a copy of his son Tommy are the exceptions that know what love is, so the chapter concludes Black Mirror is as much about a world emptied of love as about dangerous technology.

chapters.file: ch46 - Heaven is a Place on Earth.md
chapters.relation: The chapter argues Black Mirror's perception tech works because the brain constructs experience top-down (predictive coding), so implants like Playtest's mushroom, Arkangel's filter, and Men Against Fire's MASS can inject perceptions and suppress error signals - and Cooper's total VR illusion defeats every one of Descartes's strategies (memory continuity, cross-checking the senses, reason) for telling dream from reality, killing him seconds after implantation. Nozick's experience machine illuminates Danny's preference for Striking Vipers X over his marriage and Arkangel's lesson that filtering Sara's childhood perceptions left her unable to read danger or emotion. Foucault's panopticon (via Bentham) frames White Christmas's cookie interrogation modeled on real police deception (Frazier v. Cupp), the MASS implant's manufacture of 'roach' targets for killing, and Nosedive's self-imposed social ratings as modern perceptual discipline - with only trusted others (Catarina, Susan, Kelly) punching through the manipulation.

chapters.file: ch47 - 29 The Dangers of Technology in Black Mirror.md
chapters.relation: Staged as a chatroom of uploaded dead philosophers (itself a Black Museum-style cookie gimmick), the chapter stages the technology debate as Francis Bacon's optimism - technology is neutral, humans mess up, the Grain could educate and MASS could treat PTSD - against Heidegger's claim that technology is a way of thinking that turns everything, including the human mind kept on call behind the Grain and Nosedive's rated behaviors, into a resource. McLuhan's 'the medium is the message,' Benjamin's aura (he recoils at being a reproduction without aura, then a 'limited' Benjamin 2.0 embraces exhibition value and Netflix's reach), Levinas's ethics of the Other against Heidegger's ontology, Arendt's ethic of responsibility born of Nazism, and Ellul's technique - the autonomous totality of efficiency-seeking methods that enslaves us - collide over episodes from The National Anthem to Hated in the Nation, until uploading all the Greek philosophers to recover techne crashes the computer.

chapters.file: ch49 - 30 Black Mirror in the Future.md
chapters.relation: The closing essay asks whether Black Mirror will still be watched in fifty years, applying Howard Gardner's three marks of artistic beauty: interestingness (Hated in the Nation's twists), memorable form (White Bear's editing and pacing), and the invitation to revisit (Bandersnatch, which embodies it literally). Even if its 2010s gadgets come to look dated like duck-and-cover films, the chapter argues the show endures twice over - through timeliness, capturing our technological zeitgeist as Gatsby captured the Jazz Age and Guernica the Spanish Civil War, and through timelessness, since its real subject is glacially unchanging human nature grappling with change, making 'How is technology changing us?' a perennial question.

chapters.file: ch50 - Appendix How to Use This Book in the Classroom.md
chapters.relation: The editor's appendix advises instructors on teaching philosophy with Black Mirror: either watch an episode, discuss its puzzles, then read the matching chapter; or use chapters as springboards into primary literature, for example pairing Bandersnatch with van Inwagen's incompatibilism and Dennett's compatibilism on free will. Its practical heuristic - ask 'what's the technology and what's the human foible?' (the Grain magnifies Liam's paranoia, Arkangel magnifies Marie's over-parenting, Smithereens magnifies distractibility) - frames each episode as amplifying a human weakness rather than condemning technology itself.

holes.name: The Attention Economy
holes.what: An economic model (Herbert Simon) in which human attention is the scarce resource that platforms capture, optimize, and sell to advertisers - extended by Zuboff's surveillance capitalism.
holes.why: Chapter 39's entire analysis of Smithereens runs on the attention economy and behavioral surplus, and no taxonomy slug covers platforms monetizing attention.

holes.name: Gilbert Simondon
holes.what: French philosopher of technics who held that alienation arises from splitting culture from machines and that knowing our tools liberates us from the 'fetishism of the tool.'
holes.why: Chapter 39 rests its conclusion on Simondon's claim that machine-knowledge is the political answer to digital addiction, and taxonomy has no Simondon.

holes.name: René Girard
holes.what: Twentieth-century thinker of mimetic desire: we learn what to want by imitating models, which breeds rivalry with those near us.
holes.why: Chapter 40 uses Girard's mimetic desire (borrowed desire, models, external mediation) to explain Rachel's idolization of Ashley O, and taxonomy lacks Girard entirely.

holes.name: Mimetic Desire
holes.what: Girard's thesis that desire is not spontaneous but copied from models, generating emulation, idol-following and rivalry.
holes.why: Chapter 40 applies mimetic desire directly to Rachel, Jack and Ashley Too's friendship and idol dynamics, and no existing slug covers imitation-based desire.

holes.name: Transhumanism
holes.what: The movement to transcend human limits through technology - life extension, enhancement, and human-machine integration toward a posthuman state (homo technicus).
holes.why: Chapter 44 frames Be Right Back, San Junipero and the whole mortality debate through transhumanism (Kurzweil's three bridges vs Fukuyama's objection), which taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Marshall McLuhan
holes.what: Media theorist who argued 'the medium is the message': new technologies reshape human relations and perception regardless of their content.
holes.why: Chapter 47's uploaded McLuhan is a main interlocutor applying media ecology to the Grain, Black Mirror as art, and technology's dangers, with no taxonomy counterpart.

holes.name: Jacques Ellul
holes.what: Philosopher of 'technique': the autonomous totality of efficiency-seeking methods that extends beyond machines and ends by enslaving human beings.
holes.why: Chapter 47 gives Ellul's technique a central, extended voice in its dialogue on technological domination, and taxonomy has neither Ellul nor the concept of technique.

holes.name: Philosophy of Art (artistic value)
holes.what: The branch of aesthetics asking what makes something art and what gives it lasting value, e.g. Gardner/Goodman's criteria of interestingness, memorable form, and the invitation to revisit.
holes.why: Chapter 49's question of whether Black Mirror is lasting art is argued entirely through such criteria, and the taxonomy's only aesthetics slug is Kant's judgment of taste.

holes.name: Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics
holes.what: Isaac Asimov's tiered rules constraining robot harm to humans, famous as a proposed safeguard against machine danger.
holes.why: Chapter 33 seriously engages the Three Laws as robot ethics for Metalhead's robo-dogs and explains why they fail, and taxonomy has no slug for them.
